cards.title: What is a rational number?
cards.body: A number written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not 0, is a rational number. Examples: 4/5, -3/7, 0 (because 0 = 0/1). Every integer and every fraction is rational — but √2 is not, since no integer pair makes √2 = p/q.

cards.title: Standard form & numbers between
cards.body: A rational number is in standard form when its denominator is positive and p, q share no common factor: 4/6 becomes 2/3. A beautiful fact: between any two rational numbers there are INFINITELY many rational numbers — you can always find more.

cards.question: Which of these is a rational number?
cards.explanation: 3/4 = 0.75 can be written as the ratio of two integers. √2 and π cannot be written as p/q.

cards.question: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?
cards.explanation: Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many rational numbers, e.g. 3/8, 5/16, 9/32…

cards.question: What is 10/25 in standard form?
cards.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by their HCF, 5: 10÷5 = 2 and 25÷5 = 5. Standard form is 2/5.

cards.body: A rational number is p/q with q ≠ 0. Standard form divides out common factors. Between any two rationals, infinitely many more exist.

cards.title: Balance the two sides
cards.body: An equation is a statement that two sides are equal, like 2x + 3 = 9. Solving means finding the value of x that keeps the balance true. Whatever you do to one side, do the SAME to the other — that's the golden rule.

cards.title: Moving terms across (=)
cards.body: To solve 2x + 3 = 9: subtract 3 from both sides → 2x = 6, then divide both sides by 2 → x = 3. Moving a term to the other side with its sign changed (transposition) does the same job faster: +3 becomes −3.

cards.question: Solve: 3x = 15
cards.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: 3x ÷ 3 = 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

cards.question: Ravi thinks of a number. When he adds 7, he gets 12. What is the number?
cards.explanation: Let the number be x. x + 7 = 12 → x = 12 − 7 = 5.

cards.question: Solve: 2(x + 3) = 10
cards.explanation: Divide both sides by 2 → x + 3 = 5 → x = 2.

cards.body: An equation is a balance. Add, subtract, multiply or divide by the same number on both sides to find x.

cards.title: Measuring around and inside
cards.body: Mensuration measures shapes. Perimeter is length around the edge; area is the space inside (square units); volume is the space inside a solid (cubic units). For a cuboid: volume = length × breadth × height, and surface area = 2(lb + bh + lh).

cards.title: Trapezium & rhombus
cards.body: A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides: area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½(a + b)h. A rhombus has equal sides and diagonals that cut at right angles: area = ½ × d₁ × d₂.

cards.question: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 8 cm, and height 4 cm. Its area is?
A cuboid is 2 m × 3 m × 4 m. Its volume is?
cards.explanation: Volume of a cuboid = l × b × h = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 m³.

cards.question: A cube has edge 5 cm. Its volume is?
cards.explanation: Volume of a cube = side³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.

cards.body: Volume of cuboid = l × b × h; cube = side³. Trapezium area = ½(a + b)h; rhombus area = ½d₁d₂.

cards.title: Push or pull that changes things
cards.body: A force is a push or a pull. It can change the speed, direction or shape of an object. The SI unit of force is the newton (N). Forces may be contact (push, friction, muscular) or non-contact (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic) — no touching needed.

cards.title: Pressure = force ÷ area
cards.body: Pressure is the force acting on a unit area: Pressure = Force ÷ Area. A smaller area gives MORE pressure — that is why a sharp knife cuts easily, and why school bags have wide straps (less pressure on shoulders). Liquids and gases press in ALL directions.

cards.question: What is the SI unit of force?
cards.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), after Sir Isaac Newton.

cards.question: Why does a sharp knife cut easily?

options.text: Its edge has a very small area, so pressure is high

cards.explanation: Smaller area under the same force means greater pressure — Pressure = Force ÷ Area.

cards.question: Gravitational force is a ___ force.
cards.explanation: Gravity pulls objects together from a distance — no contact needed.

cards.body: Force = push or pull (unit: newton). Pressure = force ÷ area; smaller area → bigger pressure. Gravity is a non-contact force.

cards.title: Burning needs three things
cards.body: Combustion is a chemical reaction where a substance reacts with oxygen and releases heat (and often light). Three things are always needed: FUEL, OXYGEN, and the ignition temperature (the minimum temperature at which a fuel catches fire).

cards.title: Flames, fuels and calorific value
cards.body: Combustion can be rapid, spontaneous or an explosion. A candle flame has three zones; the outermost blue zone is the hottest and fully burns the fuel. Fuels differ in calorific value (heat per kg) — a good fuel has high calorific value, is easy to store and burns without much smoke.

cards.question: What are the three requirements of combustion?
cards.explanation: No oxygen → no burning. No fuel → nothing to burn. Below ignition temperature → no fire.

cards.question: Which zone of a candle flame is the hottest?
cards.explanation: The outermost zone has the most oxygen, so the fuel burns completely and the temperature is highest.

cards.question: Which of these is a solid fuel?
cards.explanation: Coal is a solid fossil fuel. Petrol and kerosene are liquids; CNG is a gas.

cards.body: Combustion needs fuel + oxygen + ignition temperature. The outer blue zone of a flame is hottest. Good fuels burn clean and give lots of heat.

cards.title: Tiny living things all around us
cards.body: Microorganisms are living organisms too small to see with the naked eye — you need a microscope. They include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and some algae; viruses are also studied here though they need a host to multiply.

cards.title: Helpful AND harmful
cards.body: Microbes help us: Lactobacillus turns milk into curd; yeast makes bread rise and ferments idli batter; Rhizobium (in the roots of legumes) fixes nitrogen; Penicillium gave us the antibiotic penicillin. They also decompose waste. But some cause diseases and spoil food — control them by salting, sugaring, oiling or pasteurisation (heating milk to 72°C).

cards.question: Which microorganism helps milk turn into curd?
cards.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, which thickens milk into curd.

cards.question: Which bacterium fixes nitrogen in the roots of leguminous plants?
cards.explanation: Rhizobium forms nodules on roots and converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.

cards.question: What is pasteurisation?
cards.explanation: Pasteurisation heats milk to about 72°C (for a short time) to destroy harmful microbes.

cards.body: Microbes are our friends (curd, bread, nitrogen, antibiotics) and sometimes foes. Preservation: salting, sugar, oil, pasteurisation.

cards.title: Anything that satisfies a need
cards.body: A resource is anything that satisfies a human need and has utility and value. Resources come from nature (air, water, soil, minerals) and from human skill. By exhaustibility they are renewable (water, solar, wind) or non-renewable (coal, petroleum, minerals).

cards.title: Ownership and conservation
cards.body: By ownership, resources are individual (a farmer’s field), community (a village pond), national (roads, ports) or international (ocean water beyond 200 nautical miles). Resources are not unlimited — sustainable development means using them so future generations also get their share.

cards.question: Which of these is a RENEWABLE resource?
cards.explanation: Solar, wind and water are renewed by nature. Coal, petroleum and gas formed over millions of years — once gone, gone.

cards.question: Minerals are classified as ___ resources.
cards.explanation: Minerals take millions of years to form, so they are non-renewable however carefully they are used.

cards.question: A village pond is an example of a ___ resource.
cards.explanation: Resources accessible to all people of a community (ponds, grazing grounds, parks) are community-owned.

cards.body: Resources = need + utility + value. Renewable vs non-renewable; individual vs community vs national. Sustainable development protects the future.

cards.title: The primary activity
cards.body: Agriculture is growing crops and raising livestock — the oldest primary activity. Arable land grows crops. Farming can be subsistence (for the farmer’s own family) or commercial (for the market).

cards.title: Kharif, Rabi and Zaid
cards.body: Crops follow the seasons. KHARIF crops are sown with the monsoon rains (June–September): rice, maize, cotton, jute. RABI crops are sown in winter (October–December): wheat, mustard, gram, peas. ZAID crops grow in the short summer between: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber. India is among the world’s largest producers of rice, wheat and sugarcane.

cards.question: Wheat and mustard are sown in which season?
cards.explanation: Wheat and mustard are rabi crops — sown after the rains, harvested in spring.

cards.question: Farming where crops are grown mainly for sale in the market is called…
cards.explanation: Commercial farming grows crops and livestock for the market to earn money.

cards.question: Which crop is grown during the kharif season?
cards.explanation: Rice is a kharif crop: it needs plenty of water from the monsoon rains.

cards.body: Agriculture = crops + livestock. Kharif (rains: rice, maize, cotton); Rabi (winter: wheat, mustard); Zaid (summer: watermelon).

cards.title: The rule book of the country
cards.body: A constitution is a body of fundamental rules that a country agrees to follow. India’s Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. It was drafted by the Constituent Assembly; Dr. B. R. Ambedkar chaired the drafting committee.

cards.title: Why we need one — key features
cards.body: A constitution builds trust in a diverse country: majorities and minorities, rulers and ruled, all agree to its rules. Key features: federalism (two levels of government), parliamentary government, separation of powers (legislature, executive, judiciary), secularism, and Fundamental Rights — including equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation.

cards.question: The Indian Constitution came into force on…
cards.explanation: Adopted on 26 Nov 1949, it took effect on Republic Day, 26 January 1950.

cards.question: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
cards.explanation: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar led the drafting committee and is called the father of the Indian Constitution.

cards.question: Which of these is a Fundamental Right in India?
cards.explanation: Fundamental Rights protect every citizen: equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural rights and constitutional remedies.

cards.body: The Constitution (26 Jan 1950) is India’s rule book: federalism, separation of powers, secularism and Fundamental Rights.

cards.title: Present · Past · Future
cards.body: Tenses tell us WHEN an action happens. Present (she goes), past (she went), future (she will go). Each has simple, continuous and perfect forms: I play, I am playing, I have played.

cards.title: Choosing the right form
cards.body: Simple present = habits (She goes to school daily). Present continuous = happening now (She is going to school). Simple past = finished (She went yesterday). Present perfect = finished but connected to now (She has finished her homework). Future uses will/shall.

cards.question: She ___ to school every day.
cards.explanation: Habits use the simple present: with he/she/it, add -s → goes.

cards.question: They ___ watching TV right now.
cards.explanation: “right now” = action in progress → present continuous: are watching.

cards.question: He ___ finished his homework (the result matters now).
cards.explanation: Present perfect expresses a completed action with present relevance: has + past participle.

cards.body: Tenses show time: present, past, future — in simple, continuous and perfect forms (go, going, gone, has gone).

cards.title: Who does it? Or who gets it?
cards.body: In ACTIVE voice the subject does the action: The cat drinks milk. In PASSIVE voice the subject receives the action: Milk is drunk by the cat. The passive is built with be + past participle.

cards.title: Three steps to convert
cards.body: To change active → passive: (1) the object becomes the subject, (2) use the correct form of be in the SAME tense, (3) write the main verb as a past participle. The cat drinks milk → Milk is drunk by the cat.

cards.question: Convert to passive: The chef cooks dinner.

options.text: Dinner is cooked by the chef.
Dinner was cooked by the chef.
The chef is cooked by dinner.

cards.explanation: Object (dinner) becomes subject; present tense be = is; cook → cooked. Dinner is cooked by the chef.

cards.question: Convert to active: The ball was hit by Ravi.

options.text: Ravi was hit by the ball.
Ravi is hitting by the ball.

cards.explanation: The doer (Ravi) becomes subject; past tense hit stays hit. Ravi hit the ball.

cards.question: Convert to passive: Ronit wrote a letter.

options.text: A letter was written by Ronit.
A letter is written by Ronit.
Ronit was written by a letter.

cards.explanation: Object (a letter) becomes subject; past tense be = was; write → written.

cards.body: Active: subject acts. Passive: subject receives — be + past participle. The object of the active becomes the subject.

cards.title: Finding the main idea
cards.body: Good readers ask questions while they read. The MAIN IDEA is the most important point the author makes. Topic sentences (often the first sentence of a paragraph) usually state it. Supporting details give examples, reasons or evidence.

cards.title: Inferring and vocabulary from context
cards.body: Sometimes the text does not say something directly — you must INFER it from clues. Words you do not know can often be guessed from the surrounding words (context clues). Read a little before and after the unknown word.

cards.question: The main idea of a paragraph is usually found in…
cards.explanation: The topic sentence (often the first) states the main point; the rest supports it.

cards.question: If you do not know a word, the BEST clue is…
cards.explanation: Context clues — surrounding words — reveal meaning.

cards.question: Inferring means…

options.text: Using clues to reach a conclusion

cards.explanation: To infer is to read between the lines using evidence in the text.

cards.body: Main idea = topic sentence. Infer = use clues. Unknown words = check context around them.
